subtopic: PROVISION TO MEET EXPENDITURES AND INDEBTEDNESS INCURRED IN 1931

speechtext:
Hon. R.. J. MANION (Minister of Railways and Canals) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 21, respecting the Canadian National
Railways, and to authorize additional provision of moneys to meet expenditures made and indebtedness incurred during the calendar year 1931.

subtopic: PROVISION TO MEET EXPENDITURES AND INDEBTEDNESS INCURRED IN 1931
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: PROVISION TO MEET EXPENDITURES AND INDEBTEDNESS INCURRED IN 1931
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill is really one which in the past has been put through the house as a supplementary estimate, where necessary, for the Canadian National Railways. The object of the bill is to authorize the Canadian National Railways to raise an additional SI 1,372,000 for the purpose of paying various accounts for the last year which the estimates of last year did not meet. This bill is introduced for the purpose of allowing the railways the S11,000,000, which they require.
Probably I had better go a little farther in my explanation because, although I was informed by my officers that there were plenty of copies of the bill, I am now informed by the Clerk of the house that they are not available. With the consent of the house I should like to proceed a little farther. The fact is that in last year's estimates the Canadian National Railways were allowed the sum of 868,000,000, and they find they now require this additional 811,000,000 odd to meet the requirements of the past year. May I read one or two clauses from the bill, which I think, explain the situation:
The net additional income deficits including bond interest but not including interest on the Dominion government advances, is $20,000,000, against which-
That is 820,000,000 extra. There was an allowance last year in the Canadian National Railways estimates for a deficit, so far as interest to the public investor was concerned, of about 831,000,000. They find however that it is in the neighbourhood of 851.000,000. It is obvious therefore that about 820,000,000 is required to cover that amount. Against that however there is S13,000,000 odd under the authority of the proviso contained in last year's bill. That proviso permitted money which was not used for other purposes, and which was contained in the estimates of last year, to be utilized if the deficit turned out to be more than the estimated deficit. That provision allowed a 813,000,000 credit against the 820,000,000 extra deficit. Then there are some smaller amounts for equipment principal payments, sinking funds, and the like, amounting to 8192,077.30. For the purchase of new equipment the amount is set at 811,014,284.11.
May I explain that the purchase of equipment by the Canadian National Railways is usually done on what is known as the Phila-
Canadian National Railways-Finances

delphia plan. A payment of 25 per cent is made, and the remaining three-quarters is financed by lien notes usually issued-in fact, I think always issued-by the banks in the United States. The Canadian National Railways carried those lien notes without the guarantee of the government. However, because of financial conditions in the world, generally, and in the United States particularly the amount of 811,000,000 cannot be borrowed in the United States to-day, and therefore it comes back as an ordinary estimate to be paid by the Dominion government. That adds another $11,000,000 odd. Against that however there is $7,331,000, which w'as borrowed last year, and which was not spent for purposes authorized. There is in this bill a clause permitting the utilization of that balance. I do not wish further to enter into the matter because figures are confusing. The result is however that a net balance of $11,000,000 is required to-day by the Canadian National Railways as a supplementary estimate.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: PROVISION TO MEET EXPENDITURES AND INDEBTEDNESS INCURRED IN 1931
speechtext:
We are most

May, however, I say quite frankly to my hon. friend that hon. gentlemen opposite have developed a habit of rushing measures into discussion in the house, and not permitting time for the due consideration which should be given. The government has a knowledge of the business of the country, and my hon. friend in particular is responsible for knowing about the business of the Canadian National Railways. If he had any reason to believe that a bill such as the one now before us would be forthcoming he might have extended some word in advance to those of us on this side of the house whom he expects to accommodate him. If the government know there are matters of importance which will have to be dealt with by a certain date, if they are anxious to expedite matters, we will try to accommodate them if they will intimate to us in advance particulars of the case. I do not think, however, it is in the public interest that measures as important as the one to which my hon. friend has just referred should be other than safeguarded by the stages of procedure provided for by the rules of the house. I do not see that this measure is going to get any more prompt consideration by passing the
second reading at the moment and having it referred to the committee of railways and shipping to-day than if that step is taken on Tuesday next, which is a government day. The bill itself is not printed, it is not distributed, and we have had no opportunity to look at it. I think my hon. friend will have to tell the railway management that there is a grave responsibility upon parliament to consider carefully every stage of Canadian National Railway financing-a responsibility that is not consistent with unduly rushing through the house measures pertaining to the railway.

subtopic: PROPOSED DEDUCTION OF TEN PER CENT IN INDEMNITIES AND SALARIES

speechtext:
Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, that it is expedient to introduce a measure to authorize deductions of ten per cent from the amounts of certain salaries or other compensations or indemnities payable by the government of Canada during the fiscal year 1932-33.
And to provide for payment out of the consolidated revenue fund of all current contributions payable under the provisions of the Civil Service Superannuation Act in respect of the salaries payable during the fiscal year ending March 31, 1933, of all employees who receive not more than one thousand two hundred dollars per annum.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in moving that you do now leave the chair to enable the house to resolve itself into a committee of the whole to consider the resolution which has just been read, I do so in the absence of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) who is still indisposed and confined to his bed. Since the opposition have indicated that they do not propose to consider items concerning salaries in the estimates of the two departments now before the committee of supply
[Mr. McIntosh.J
until such time as the policy of the government has been made known with respect to the reduction of civil service salaries by ten per cent, I am moving this motion in the place and stead of the Minister of Finance. I greatly regret that it falls to my duty to do so, because the Minister of Finance had prepared himself more adequately than I to explain the resolution to the house.
I should like to preface anything I have to say by the observation that the civil service of this country has now become a very large body; approximately 65,000 people are affected by this resolution. The civil service is a body of which this country has become justly proud, because there are many employees in the service who discharge onerous and difficult duties with credit and distinction. On the other hand it is beyond question that the service has become overmanned in many departments. That, I think, is a commonplace. That the Beatty commission, charged in 1930 with the responsibility of determining the extent to which the service could be reduced or improved, has not made a report is well known to every hon. member of this house, but that there are larger numbers on the payroll of the country than the necessities demand I think has been felt by every thoughtful investigator for many years.
That does not detract from the value of the service that is rendered by the painstaking and thoughtful men and women who serve the state with loyalty and who do not look upon their positions merely as opportunities to enable them to see what they can get from the treasury, but there are those who do take that attitude, and ultimately that matter must be determined by suitable and proper investigation. After all, the civil servants of this country are the instruments by which the business of government is carried on, just as in every business there are employees, clerks, managers and executive heads, for the purpose of directing the activities of that business. So the state through its government has the right, which it exercises, of employing from time to time men and women to discharge the obligations that are necessary for the conduct of public business, and as I have said, in the main these duties have been discharged satisfactorily to the Canadian people.
During the last few days we have had much discussion as to the principles that should govern in appointments to the service, in promotions and in the payment of compensation for services rendered. The committee that was appointed, and that reported upon professional compensation, indicated that in their opinion the professional class, having

Public Service-Salary Deduction
regard to the salaries commanded in other walks of life, were not adequately compensated, and certain recommendations were made. I think it goes without saying, and at least my observations lead me to believe, that there is no question at all as to the fact that there are certain classes of the public service that are not adequately paid. They could command a larger compensation in other walks of life, yet in these days it is apparent that the compensation given is not so much out of line as some people have thought. There is a measure of security of employment; there is a certainty of not too long hours and there is also provision for a pension. To this the individual makes a contribution, but he does not pay the whole cost; the state itself makes continuous contributions from year to year to the superannuation funds in order that these pensions may be paid.
Then, of course, there is the other class which, in the opinion of most people, is overpaid. It is not my purpose, however, to do more than say that that is a matter which will be subsequently investigated at an opportune time. The principle upon which compensation has been awarded in the past and salaries paid has been, in my judgment at least, too elastic to bring about reasonably proper results. I know of salaries that are being paid to those in the service which are out of all proportion to the salaries paid to others also in the service. Those who are receiving, for instance, $250 a month or $220 a month, as compared with those who receive $150, are not called upon to discharge, nor do they discharge obligations a*t all commensurate with the difference between the two levels of salary.
Leaving that for the moment, we find that during the last two years, owing to the great pressure of depression upon the public purse, and owing to the difficulty of raising taxes beyond a certain measure, there has been, not only on the part of governments but by private enterprises, an effort to curtail and, by the practice of economies, to restore a balance between income and outgoings. The Canadian Pacific Railway Company a year ago instituted such economies; the Canadian National Railways last year instituted economies in that direction; and further economies have been effected by the findings of boards in connection with the running trades. Recently a board was sitting in Montreal when its duties were suddenly ended by an agreement being arrived at whereby a ten per cent reduction was accepted by the clerical staffs of the railways, the question then being 41761-36
under consideration by a conciliation board. In private enterprises throughout the country, apart from the great transportation companies, the same principle has been followed. The public service is called upon, therefore, to consider the conditions that now exist in the light of the treatment accorded by other employers to their employees, which has been governed not only by the economic necessities of the various enterprises to which I have referred but also by the fact that there has been a considerable reduction in the cost of living. The figures furnished by the Department of Labour indicate that at the present time the cost of living, as compared with 1926, is as follows: Food costs, a reduction of 30-4 per cent; fuel costs, a reduction of 5-8 per cent; rent, rs of 1 per cent; clothing, 23-6 per cent, and sundries, 2-2 per cent. Weighted, as is done by statisticians in an endeavour to arrive at an average comparable with other averages, the average given is 14-4 per cent; and so far as wages and salaries generally are concerned, the statisticians report that the average reduction throughout the country is approximately ten per cent, or perhaps a little more.
The proposals contained in this resolution contemplate a reduction of compensation awarded to the public service of ten per cent in the case of all those who receive upwards of $1,200 per annum, and inasmuch as under $1,200 a ten per cent reduction might effect some hardships, the state or the treasury is absorbing the five per cent for superannuation, leaving the net contribution made by the individual receiving $1,200 or less per annum five per cent of his annual salary. In other words, if he receives $1,200 per annum his contribution to the welfare of Canada will be $60 or $5 per month. That applies to all classes and all persons except the representatives of the crown, judges, and the members of the military, naval and air forces, and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. It will include all payments, regardless of designation. Some employees receive regular salaries plus various allowances payable either in cash or in kind. These additional payments may be designated as salaries or allowances, or other similar terms may be used; but if they form part of the remuneration attached to the office they will be subject to the ten per cent reduction. I may say that where living allowances are provided for, obviously the living allowance would not be included in the amount from which the ten per cent would be deducted. But where there is a sum added to another sum for the purpose of determining the amount upon which the superannuation

Public Service-Salary Deduction
allowance is paid, then that will be the sum from which the ten per cent reduction will be made. In other words, everything that is received by the individual that might be classified as remuneration, compensation or salary, for the purpose of enabling the contribution to the superannuation fund to be determined, will be the sum or the amount from which the ten per cent will be deducted.
So far as the exceptions are concerned, the representatives of the crown in the various provinces are not subject to that deduction; and those of us who are familiar with the costs and expense involved by any Canadian who has accepted the office of lieutenant governor will agree, I think, that although he pays income tax upon that sum he has not-at least so far as I have been able to ascertain-[DOT] except in one province ever been able to succeed in maintaining the office on that sum or in fact on one very much larger. The judges are not included in this measure. It has been contended by legal authority, and an article in the last issue of the Law Quarterly Review goes into the matter rather fully, that it would be a breach of the statutory rights of judges to undertake to make a curtailment in their salaries in this way. There are, however, other methods by which the matter may be dealt with, and the government has not finally determined what action it may take in that regard. The ten per cent reduction will also apply to all those bodies or agents or trustees of the government that are discharging functions in the name of or for the government-for instance, the grain commissioners, the railway commissioners, the harbour commissioners. Obviously, however, there is no jurisdiction on the part of this administration or of any government to impose this reduction, if it is so called, upon the employees of the Canadian National Railways. They are dealt with by their own organizations-that is, the executive of the railway itself. But I should like to make it clear that the ten per cent reduction will apply in all other cases of employees of the public service, direct or indirect, with the exceptions I have just mentioned.
Superannuation benefits will not be affected. The contributors will make their contributions on the salaries received after deducting the ten per cent, and those retired will receive benefits based on the regular compensation rates before the reduction.

I am merely pointing out that, despite that, I believe the great body of opinion of the civil service leans to the view that this is not an unreasonable contribution to make under present conditions, nor will it lie within the mouths of those who oppose this measure to charge that there has been reckless expenditure of public moneys, for whatever else may be said, every department of the public service up to this moment has lived well within the estimates voted at the last session, which were substantially less than the estimates of the previous year which were not prepared by the present administration. What is more, I think it will be found as the session progresses that there has been a real and vigorous effort to effect economies in the public service, and if these economies are not popular and do not conduce to the popularity of the administration, we conceive our duty to be far greater than that which is involved in the popularity of a government. From day to day, week to week and month to month we have continued to discharge the duties which devolve upon us, endeavouring not only to maintain the economic structure of this country and its credit, but to enable it to meet its obligations in every part of the world in the terms of the contracts creating them.
In addition to that we have been called upon to support, financially and otherwise, the western provinces of this confederation so that, despite the extraordinary depression through which they are passing and the difficulties they have to encounter, their credit may be maintained. Now, at the very threshold of a new year, so far as crops are concerned, we are confronted with the request that not thousands or hundreds of thousands of dollars be provided, but that millions of dollars be provided to enable the husbandmen between the lakes and the mountains again to sow their seed, trusting to the harvest which, for the last three years, has not resulted from their efforts. These are the difficulties under which we live; these are the difficulties under which we carry on. And we believe that when there is an understanding-as there will be- as to just what the situation is, hon. gentlemen who sit apposite will not be proud of any opposition they have urged against efforts made to provide, by methods indicated, a contribution to the welfare of this country to maintain its integrity and existence as a dominion in a time of the greatest stress through which the ship of state has laboured.
We believe that, and we are content to leave the issue with those who ultimately are to decide it. We have gone forward and discharged an unpleasant task, an unhappy task. We realized the responsibilities placed upon us because of conditions which are now worldwide, and are known by every thoughtful man to be universal, that are not measured in terms of what took place in 1929, 1930 or any other year, conditions the like of which have never been known to the mind of men. Realizing all that, we have endeavoured, Mr. Speaker, to the best of our ability, to provide that there shall be a balanced budget brought about by economies and by the utmost care in the public estimates, there being reductions in them such as this house has never witnessed before, and to which we hope to give effect. The taxation we 'believe will not be so unreasonable as to shatter the hope and courage of the Canadian people, because there is a limit to what a new people in a new country numbering only about 10,000,000 can stand.
Realizing all these considerations, we submit this resolution to the house in the earnest hope that it may be considered fairly, free from prejudice or any efforts directed towards political advantage, seeing in it what it really is-a measure for the purpose of adding to the revenue of this country without doing hardship to any person. We have felt that a class which has received protection and security through all the years should make a definite contribution to the revenues of Canada, and I feel certain, as I said to the representatives at the meeting this morning, that as they do it gladly, when these dark clouds have passed away and this time is forgotten, they will look back with pleasurable pride upon the contribution they have made to the prosperity of the country they love so well.

Hon. gentlemen opposite say "hear, hear." Now, assuming that that is true, are we to understand that this is a measure for cutting down the public service of Canada? Because if it is it is a very different measure from what I have understood it to be up to the present time. I have regarded this as a measure for a percentage deduction from the existing salaries of those in the public service; I have not regarded it as a measure to lessen the total number of persons in the public service. I do not say that an investigation to that end might not be very profitably held and economies effected where it may be possible, but I do take exception to having the public assume from the words of the Prime Minister that he at the present time under this measure is trying to reduce the public service, when as a matter of fact so far as the measure itself extends it will not reduce the size of the service by a single individual.
My right hon. friend spoke of some salaries being out of all proportion to the work or service being rendered in some positions in comparison with the work or service being rendered in other positions. That may be perfectly true, but I do not understand this measure to be one having to do with any readjustment of salaries. It has nothing whatever to do with that, and I do not see why my right hon. friend in his remarks should seek to convey to the country an impression that his government is dealing with that particular matter in this particular resolution. Because they are not doing anything of the kind.
My right hon. friend also spoke of the economies which are being sought to be effected in the public service. Are we to understand that this is a measure for effecting in the public service, economies which will continue through the years, or is it, as it purports to be and what my right hon. friend in his concluding remarks said it was, a measure to occasion a deduction of a portion of the salaries for one year only? If it is a measure to effect economy in the public service, that would imply that these salaries are being reduced with a view to having them permanently maintained at a lower level. I say the ministry in that regard cannot be too emphatic or too clear in making its exact position known.

I gathered from the concluding remarks of my right hon. friend that it is not intended by this measure to bring about in any way a permanent reduction in the level of salaries throughout the public service; I take that from his statement that this measure would have effect only until March 31 of next year. The Prime Minister says it will have no vigour of life beyond that date. Again I should like to accept the Prime Minister's word, but I am not too sure of what may happen at the end of that time, and I refer to it at this moment in order that there may be some record of this aspect having been considered at this time. I speak as I do because on this very order paper of to-day there is notice of motion that on Monday next we consider the amending of an act passed last year so as to extend its provisions from the month of March to the month of May of this year. When the measure to which I have just referred was before parliament last year we were told in very plain language that it would expire on March 1 of this year; at that time the Prime Minister was quite emphatic that the provisions of the measure would not apply beyond that date. He stated that parliament would be in session when March came around and there would be no need for extending the measure beyond that time. So I say, with that motion on the order paper, indicating a position diametrically opposite to that which my right hon. friend took at the time of the introduction of the measure, we must be particuarly cautious in accepting my right hon. friend's words as to the length of time for which the present measure will be in force. Some of these civil servants, both high and low, gave themselves to the service of the country yearn ago; a great many of them have rendered faithful service; now, without any consultation, without their being given any chance in any way to make modifications, they are suddenly deprived of the right to their statutory increases and, in addition, have their salaries cut ten per cent. It seems to me if there is any idea of keeping contracts we are bound to keep contracts of this kind. I am not one of those who think a contract should be forever binding. It seems to me, with the variations which take place in our general social arrangements, and especially with the variations which have taken place in .recent years in the purchasing power of money, that all contracts should be subject to frequent revision; that is the only fair thing under the circumstances. But I cannot see the slightest reason why anyone should urge that the salaries of particular groups cannot be changed because they are statutory, while those of other groups may be changed ait will.
One of the most serious features about these cuts-and I have no doubt it is one of the reasons why they have been made-is the effect on employees outside the civil service. To no small extent this action by the government will be taken as an excuse for employers all over the country to reduce salaries. This is not merely an evil when looked at from the standpoint of the individual employee; more than that it is an aggravation of the disease with which we are now afflicted. The trouble to-day is the lack of purchasing power. I think the residents of the city of Ottawa are being taught a very salutary lesson in economics, because they are learning that this cut in the payroll means so many million dollars leas to the local shopkeepers. What is true in local matters is equally true right across the country. If we had an increase in public works, and in salary expenditure it would mean an increase in purchasing .power, and it might possibly start the wheels of industry moving again.
I know that looked at from the standpoint of the government in an effort to balance its budget something must be done, and I know the Prime Minister, looking at the matter from the standpoint of his own business, may say: Well, we have to slash; this is the only way we manage to balance our budget in our

It is quite true that economy may be a good thing for .me as an individual. But it is equally true that economy practised by a government and on a wholesale scale is to-day a fatal thing, as is recognized by all the loading authorities on economics. A government at a time of crisis, of trade slackness, should stand behind any movement to increase the general purchasing power of the people, it should embark on public works and other undertakings to supplement what is being done by private individuals. That is the only way in which this private competitive system may continue to run, because under this system we 'have always had these slack periods, and if these slack periods are in any sense to be ironed out, it must be by a central government. But our government is doing precisely the same thing that every private employer is doing-cutting right and left. The economic effect will be disastrous.

As my colleague suggests, they are going sky high, for after all the decrease in dividends of the big concerns is not very marked. For instance, the decreased .percentage paid by the banks is not very substantial; they are keeping well up to their regular average. Yes, but his interest on it at 5 or 6 per cent is worth to-day in its purchasing power almost twice what it was at the time the bond was issued.

Still another method might be adopted. I am not sure that I agree altogether with my hon. friend from Macleod (Mr. Coote), but I am inclined to think that a very considerable measure of inflation might be an even fairer thing than the income tax. Leaving aside the question of its ultimate economic effects, I think perhaps a measure of inflation would be the fairest way all round, since that would allow those people who have money to-day to get the real value of that money and not a fictitious value.
Let me come back for a moment to where I was when the Prime Minister interjected his question. It seems to me that to-day we should levy our taxes upon those who have money. They are enjoying their wealth because of privileges of some kind or another, and because of the protection of the state. It has been said that if we had not had the war we would have had no wealth in this country. Those people have enjoyed whatever benefit there has come from the war, though I believe it has been precious little. They are enjoying all the protection of ordered government; in a great many cases they are enjoying special legislation which has enabled them to make money. I make that statement without any reservation and I will give my reasons very shortly.
In the first place, you cannot possibly impose a straight flat rate of reduction like ten per cent, or any other percentage for that matter, on all civil servants regardless of whether they get SI ,000 or $20,000. It is utterly unfair; I have never heard of such a proposal either in war time or in peace time. Why impose it now? It is said that the ship of state is in danger. Well, are you going to cripple the crew numerically or degrade it in any way if you want to save the ship? Yet that is what is being done by this resolution at this critical time in the history of the country. Would not the government be better employed strengthening instead of weakening the civil service as they are doing in this proposed legislation?
I have another protest against the resolution and that is that it is intended as a mere sop to those of the civil service who receive salaries of less than $1,200 a year; it is-offered them as a means of making them satisfied with a ten per cent reduction. They are supposed to feel that it is all right because they will get half of it back. But do all of them get it back? From inquiries I have been able to make, inquiries not yet fully complete, about -two of them will get the five per cent back for every one who will suffer the full ten per cent reduction. The fact is, many are not eligible for the superannuation subsidy which is proposed in this resolution because they are not insured. Now, what is the sense of giving them something with one hand and taking it back with the other? Why not start off with a small cut and graduate the reduction as applying to the service generally? Instead of doing that the government are merely pretending to give with one hand while they are taking away with the other. I object to this most strenuously. As I say, it is merely a sop, a safety sop intended to save the face of the government in introducing a proposal for a straight flat reduction of ten per cent that cannot be defended by any body of representatives such as this.

As far as an effort to attain something is concerned, they are leaning upon the civil service for help in the working out of their policy.

Why not have a capital levy in this country if we need $10,000,000 or $15,000,000 or $20,000,000 to balance the budget as we do? I think the Canadian people realize why we need money to balance the budget to-day. The reason is that the fiscal policy of the present administration has been a bungle; that we are in the hole financially and that we must now ask the civil servants to come through with a cut of ten per cent to help balance the budget by giving a total of $8,000,000 or $10,000,000. Why not go after the millionaires who have unproductive capital, who are not using this money in a productive way, and get your $10,000,000 or $20,000,000 or $100,000,000? Why not go out after the big fellows who have the money and who are not using it to build up Canada as they might, rather than after the men who are receiving a small salary, who have not had their statutory increases during the last year and who have on their hands obligations which they must meet? I would think there is an avenue there along which we might profitably go in order to get all the money we want. More than that, we would be asking the men who can pay to put up their money. If the men who have their money in unproductive channels to-day and who love Canada and are patriotic

One w.ay to strengthen the economic structure of Canada would be to put into effect a brand new tariff policy, to remove the high protection that we have at the present time and to give the country a breathing space in a commercial way, in a trading way, thereby helping to balance our budget by developing and building up international trade.

Mr. Speaker, I desire to detain the house only a very few moments in connection with this resolution. At the outset I should like to say to those who have spent their lives in efforts to improve the conditions of working men and women and to provide employment for them, a reduction of wage rates or of salaries is never a pleasant thing, or a move in which we like to participate. But in relation to the situation with which we are faced today, representing as I do a constituency composed entirely of working men and farmers, I should like to say that in my judgment nothing this government has done or can do will receive greater commendation throughout the country than the action they are taking in reducing the salaries of all public servants, who must be paid from money contributed by the working men and the farmers of this country.
I have a picture before me of the men and women in the constituency I represent, railway employees, men working in lumber camps and in mines, and farmers throughout the scattered parts of the district. These men are harassed every day of their lives, because of conditions at present prevailing, to meet their tax bills; and after all these are the people who must pay taxes. A great deal has been said about starting at the top, taxing the large incomes, taking away the money from those who have it. I should like to say to the house, from the slight knowledge I have of general business conditions throughout this country, that the income tax receipts will be very much less in the year ahead of us, and in the year following, than they have been in the past. The higher you endeavour to put
the income tax the less you will get from it, because the men who are presumed to have these large incomes in many cases are not earning incomes at all. There is no class of men in this country who are finding it more difficult to meet the situation than those who are presumed to be the wealthy men, responsible for endeavouring to carry on industry in this country.
Let me return for a moment to the people whom I represent, the farmers in nor1 hern Ontario who are struggling every day and every night to meet the situation with which they are confronted. They are forced to pay their proportion of the taxes out of which the salaries of all civil servants in this country are paid. The workingmen are in the same position, and when I go back to my constituency, as I am going to-night and meet these workingmen face to face, I know exactly what will be their viewpoint. Already they have been forced to accept very severe cuts in their wages; it could not be otherwise. Hon. members speak as though a business man, an employer of labour, can fix his rates of wages high or low, just as he chooses; they seem to think that the farmer who must go out and employ labour on his farm can do the same thing. It matters not which it is; they can pay their employees only what they receive for the goods they are producing, and they cannot pay more. For example how will the Canadian National Railway pay its income tax during 1932 and 1933? Where is it going to get the money with which to pay the salaries and wages that must be paid? The rates of wages have been cut, and how could it be otherwise? The only alternative would have been to add to the taxes of this country ; that is exactly what it involved. Let me repeat that no one likes to see salaries reduced. I ain one of those anxious to spe working men and women get the highest rate of remuneration it is possible for them to receive, but we are faced with a situation which makes that impossible. Where are we to get the money for them?
Something has been said about reducing the interest rates on government bonds hold in Canada. An hon. member of this house undertook this afternoon to prove that a widow, if you like, who is receiving an income from bonds which she purchased from the proceeds of an insurance policy, could buy more goods with each dollar she received from that source than a workingman could buy with the dollar he received for working in a factory, a mine, the woods or anywhere else. A more ridiculous proposition could not be suggested. Let me ask this:	From whom
would this money be taken if we repudiated

Mr. Speaker, I want to take up
the time of the house very shortly in connection with the principle of the resolution which the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) has proposed shall be considered in committee of the whole. The principle to which we on this side of the house particularly object is the principle of a horizontal and arbitrary cut regardless of the size of salary affected. That is a principle which has been too freely adopted by this government in connection with other measures affecting the public service and the administration of government.
Our complaint-and we will continue to make it-is that our friends on the other side seem willing to take a running jump at almost 41761-38
any policy and put it into effect, and then sometimes take a step backward and make some corrections, or at other times-and more frequently-to stick to it through thick and thin, with resulting detriment to the people affected. I submit that in this case the government have already shown that they are not quite happy with regard to the proposal made by the Prime Minister some little time ago, the proposal which appears in the estimates, whereby ten per cent is simply cut off every civil government vote. Already they have begun to take a backward step in the second part of the resolution before the house. My hon. friend from Carleton (Mr. Garland), who spoke a short time ago, mentioned politics, and the Prime Minister spoke of introducing politics into this matter. I wonder if perhaps it was not because the civil servants have votes that this second paragraph was included. Does anyone think that paragraph would have appeared had it not been for the fact that hon. gentlemen opposite are just as sensitive to public opinion when expressed through the polls as anyone else in this house or in this country? I say, Mr. Speaker, that the second part of the resolution, the sop which is now thrown by way of contributing five per cent towards the superannuation funds of certain officials, is an attempt by the government to take a step backward, and is an admission that they went too far.
That has only come about because the opposition have steadfastly set their faces against the voting of any estimates which recognize salary cuts until this resolution and this legislation should be brought down, and already we see the fruits of that policy. I submit that it should be elementary in government and in the administration of public affairs, particularly in taxation, that taxes should be imposed on those best able to bear them. This is nothing but a taxation measure which is imposed upon a certain class in the community because they happen to be civil servants. There is an old adage about tempering the wind to the shorn lamb, but that was completely forgotten in the proposal first announced by the Prime Minister.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the arbitrary way in which this government went at this matter is just an illustration of what has been done with regard to other matters, to which I will not refer to-night. Can you conceive of anything less fair and more inequitable than that the people who are to be affected should see it broadcast all over this country that the ten per cent .cut was going into effect, have the estimates brought down with

They appeared this morning, by their representatives, to present their case, while upon this very order paper was the resolution providing for the reduction in salary, and I have no doubt that the bill to be founded upon this resolution has been already printed. You might as well speak of a court giving people an opportunity to bring their witnesses and present their case while all the time the judgment of the court is written, ready to be pronounced as soon as the presentation ends.
My hon. friend from Carleton pretends to speak for the civil servants; he says they are perfectly willing to take this cut. I sincerely hope that is so, because it looks as if they are going to get it whether they want to take it or not. But I do say that I doubt very much whether he is in a position to speak for the civil servants and to say whether the reduction is one that does approve itself, particularly as regards the feature to which I am referring, to the great body of civil servants of the country.
This principle is all wrong, of imposing a horizontal cut in salaries regardless of their size. Suppose a man receives a salary of $720 a year; he has to contribute the sum of $06 to the revenue of the country. Does anyone pretend for a moment that a man can as well afford to contribute $96 out of an income of $720 as the man drawing a salary of $10,000 can afford to contribute $1,000? There is certainly a scale of living in this country which is absolutely necessary. Certain absolute requisites a man must have if he is to keep his family, and these things must be provided first. As was well said by my hon. friend from North Battleford (Mr. McIntosh), the principle seems to be to start from the bottom and work upwards instead of from the top down. What is being done by the government with respect to the reduction in salaries is precisely the same sort of thing that has been carried on right along; it is exactly the same thing as was done by the Minister of National Defence and by the government in connection with the air men of whom I spoke the other day. That is an illustration of the arbitrary way in which our friends opposite are acting in regard to matters of taxation and these so-called economies.
The Prime Minister read a letter which he said came from some lady who wrote that she was glad to have a salary to be cut. I am sorry the right hon. gentleman is not in his seat, but I would *ask him whether as a lawyer he regards this as the proper sort of

evidence to bring against the great body of civil servants of the country-a letter written by a lady whose name he will not give, whose condition of employment we know nothing about, about whose responsibilities in life we are absolutely ignorant, -when I venture to say that the Prime Minister himself, in common with others in this house, has received letters by the score from civil servants all over the country protesting vigorously against the cut because of what it will mean to them in their daily lives. I say to the right hon. gentleman, and I submit to the house, that he should not have brought forward a letter of that kind, an isolated case, and presented it to this house or to the country as an evidence of the way in which the civil servants of Canada generally feel in this matter.
Misery likes company, we know, and we are all receiving the cut; but everyone has been suggesting that someone else should make sacrifices. It reminds one of what Mark Twain said about being perfectly willing to sacrifice his wife's relations. In this case, the lady to whom reference has been made might sincerely have felt like making the contribution; but there are a lot of married men in this city and throughout the country with large families and very grave responsibilities, who cannot afford the cut no matter how patriotic they are. I have spoken of the air force as an example of the arbitrary actions of the government. My hon. friends opposite rush headlong at salaries, striking off ten per cent, and it means headlines in the papers the next day and possibly some applause in some quarters. But is it scientific? Is it intelligent? Is it considerate? Is it a thing that ought to be done in the interests of public business? Take the men in the air force; they were officers who were under contract for three years, men who had enlisted for that length of service, men who had seen service overseas, half of them married men with family responsibilities who had expected that their employment would be fairly permanent and many of them on the strength of that expectation had acquired little homes of their own. They have no other profession than their training in the air force and they were working for their country to the very best of their ability. These men receive summary notice that in six weeks' time they are to be cut off the salary list altogether and they find themselves adrift in the world without any support whatever. Now, that is not the way to use Canadians. What would any employer of labour have done?

This is what he has done. He has said to his superintendent or his supervisor:	We have to reduce our staff. Show
me the married men; tell me who have been longest with the firm; point out those who have responsibilities, and then we will try to temper the wind to the shorn lamb, endeavouring as far as possible to adjust matters, dropping some who have not as great responsibilities, and others who have not been as long with us, or who have not had service overseas. That is what the employer of labour has done. But he has not made an absolute brutal and ruthless cut or dismissal regardless of salaries, contracts, abilities and responsibilities. And I say that is what is being done. It is because my hon. friends opposite do not realize that there is such a thing as human flesh and blood in this country as well as questions of economics and all the other things they talk about in connection with government. They say, "we are going to do this and that or perish in the attempt," and they do it regardless of whom it hits.
I submit that the time has come in this country when we ought to call a halt to that sort of thing. My hon. friend from Temis-couata (Mr. Pouliot) gave some excellent advice. It would be well for the country if the government would stop for the space of just one day and give consideration quietly and soberly to the things that are being done instead of rushing at them, particularly in regard to these so-called economies. After all, we are dealing with human beings, Canadian citizens, and when you reduce by ten per cent the income of a man who gets $720 a year, or when you throw out into the world a man who has served his country well, it is time to point out that the same sort of human feeling and sensibilities that move the employer of labour should actuate the government.
Coming back to the air men, may I point out that the only employment open to these men in Canada at the present time is with the federal government. I would not mind it so much if there were not plenty of work for them to do and if they were not needed in the service of the country for the development of its resources. But I have seen, as other members of this house have seen, the excellent work which has been done by the air service, rvork which could not have been done, in the development of this country, without their invaluable assistance. There is not a country I know of that has made such a varied use of aviation as this dominion has done in connection with the development of our natural resources. Let me give one or two illustrations to indicate what little
consideration has really been devoted to these matters. One would have thought that the government would first have considered the usefulness of these men and what they are doing in the development of this country. Hon. members know that the air force has been used most successfully in connection with the mapping of the country and the opening-out of new mining areas. You could not lay off mining areas, you could not plot them, you could not allot them nor stake them ou't without a map. Take the Red Lake district for example. Three or four years ago there was a request that it be opened up. A request came for a map of the district. How long would it take to make such a map by means of ordinary foot survey? About three years. The matter was handed over to the Department of the Interior and through that department to the air force, and the map was ready in a space of a little more than six months. The claims were staked out and the district was opened for development. I have in mind an engineer who wanted to make an inspection in that district. He was coming from Vancouver, having been asked by his firm to make an examination. He knows that from the time he gets off the train at Minaki until he gets on again it will take three weeks to go into the district and out again by the usual method. He wires for a plane, the plane meets him at Minaki and takes him into the Red Lake district, and he makes his examination and catches the very same train the very same day at Sioux Lookout and is on his way to New York-all this by reason of the aviation service rendered by these very men who have been dropped because the government gives no thought to their usefulness in the development of Canada.
With regard to the great northwest, of which you know a good deal, Mr. Speaker, we have lately had mineral discoveries of importance at Great Bear lake. I have no doubt that the Department of Mines will bear out the statement that it is absolutely *necessary that we maintain our air service if we are to develop that country. The same thing may be said in connection with the air mail service. Civil government aviators developed air mail routes throughout the country, investigated conditions, mapped out the courses, provided the necessary information to enable contracts to be let, made experimental flights themselves, selected sites for emergency landing fields and laid the foundation for a splendid airmail service in this country of vast distances. A similar statement may be made in connection with

Therefore I say that being the case, the wage earners of Canada, whether civil servants or otherwise, must expect to make some sacrifice on behalf of their country. And a large proportion of other wage earners have made sacrifices. The two great railway systems last year made cuts in the salaries of their higher-up officers by, I think, ten per cent, representing a reduction of some millions of dollars. More recently they came to an agreement with the running trades to accept a reduction of ten per cent. That is a fairly drastic cut. That amount of wealth less in the pockets of our people means a lower standard of living, and my right hon. friend cannot get away from that. WThen we voted for a higher tariff, we voted for a lower standard of living. Tariffs cannot be raised without the cutting of wages and the producing of lower standards of living.

Mr. Speaker, when the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) was addressing the house he alluded to the fact that the railroad employees and those employed by private interests had been forced to take a reduction in their wages. I am sorry that the present government has had to follow the lead of private interests. I have been brought up to think a government should be an ideal employer and take the lead in showing how employees ought to be treated, but in this instance we have the government following the lead of private employers in Canada in reducing wages. I am sorry, however, the government has not followed the example set by private employers in this country in taking the employees or their representatives into their confidence and discussing the matter with them before introducing legislation such as is now before the house.
This parliament has several times enunciated the principle of collective bargaining. Indeed, some of the members who are to-day sitting on the treasury benches were members of the government in 1918 when they enunciated in an order in council this principle. Order in council P.C. 1743 of July 11, 1918, reads in section two:
That all employees have the right to organize in trade unions, and this right shall not be denied or interfered with in any manner whatsoever, and through their chosen representatives should be permitted and encouraged to negotiate with employers concerning working conditions, rates of pay, or other grievances.
That principle was adopted by the government of Canada on July 11, 1918, during the war. After the war was over, on the first of May, 1919, some members now sitting on the treasury benches were members of the government that passed another order in council cancelling some of the provisions in the former one, but leaving intact the particular clause which I have just read.
Then parliament endorsed the principle of collective bargaining and endorsed unanimously the principle of establishing a national council for the civil service of Canada. In conformity with that endorsation the former Liberal government on the seventh of May, 1930, passed the following order in council, P.C. 970:
The committee of the Privy Council have had before them a report, dated 6th May, 1930, from the Minister of Labour, directing attention to the Votes and Proceedings of the House of Commons of Tuesday, March 27, 1928, and

Thursday, March 29, 1928; and more specifically to the second report presented to the house from the select standing committee on industrial and international relations and to the record of the adoption of the said report by the house, contained therein.
It will be observed that by adopting the said report the house endorsed "the principle of the establishment by the government of a national civil service council, composed of representatives of the government and the organized civil service in equal numbers, to consider and advise the government upon matters of mutual concern to the government and civil servants in their respective capacities as employer and employees, also as to the establishing of any other consultative and advisory machinery that may be required." And further, the house agreed "that, as the form of constitution for such a council, covering its scope and functions, can best be determined by joint agreement between the parties concerned," a committee should be set up by the government, representing both the government and the civil service organizations, to draft a constitution for such a national civil service council, any such constitution to be subject to the approval of the governor in council.
Haying in mind the foregoing, the minister submits that the time would now appear appropriate for the taking of the initial step suggested by the report above quoted.
The committee, therefore, submit for Your Excellency's approval the following recommendations of the Minister of Labour.
1.	That a national civil service council drafting committee should forthwith be constituted, to draft a constitution for a national civil service council.
2.	In establishing such a committee there first arises the question of its membership. The policy of giving equal representation to civil service organizations and to the government should be observed.
3.	Representation of civil service organizations:
The Department of Labour has record of some twenty-eight organizations of civil servants throughout the country, varying in respect of their memberships from about seventeen to over 8,000. Obviously, with such a comparatively large number of organizations existing, giving direct representation to them all ivould not be practicable, in view of the fact that the setting up of a committee of at least fifty-six members would be involved thereby. Selecting those organizations reporting 500 or more members, it is observed that there are ten which fall into this category. These organizations represent substantially all classes of civil servants organized, covering practically all branches of the service in which there is organization, and they include an overwhelming majority of the organized civil service. These ten organizations should be given representation on the committee. While not directly represented under this plan, several of the smaller organizations will be represented through affiliation with one or other of the larger bodies. In order to represent as many bodies as may be possible while still limiting the size of the committee to a reasonable figure, numerical differences among organizations should be overlooked rvhen determining representation, and if each of these ten organizations had one representative to speak for it, even though these differences in size exist, the representation
